rationale: Both are high-value primary scientific records, but one is astronomical source astrometry and the other paleontological specimens. The useful relationship is preservation architecture: future interpretations must remain derivatives of preserved primary observations.

Both preserve machine-readable inputs/outputs useful for future reanalysis. Astrometric propagation and atmospheric simulation are different domains, so the relationship is methodological rather than substantive.

Both digitized records combine primary specimens/observations with modern taxonomic interpretation. They demonstrate a reusable separation between original evidence and versioned taxonomic conclusions.

The new species treatment can potentially improve taxonomic identity resolution in plant-interaction datasets; this is an opportunity for taxonomic crosswalks, not evidence that the species participates in a particular bee interaction.

Both are large occurrence archives derived from observational communities. Their explicit quality flags can be compared to understand missing coordinates, taxonomic uncertainty and sampling bias without treating either archive as ground truth.
The OBIS marine subset and NOAA NEFSC visual survey can provide complementary spatial coverage while preserving different observation designs, effort structures and quality controls.

Both concern atmospheric/environmental measurement systems and uncertainty, but one is modeled microplastic transport and the other sensor intercomparison. The connection is methodological and supports future measurement-model comparison.

Both are RKI national surveillance products with explicit reporting frameworks. They can be compared as surveillance-system objects while preserving disease-specific definitions and reporting processes.

Both describe COVID-19 surveillance but represent different outcome streams. Linking them supports temporal and reporting-delay analysis only when denominators, reporting dates and nowcast methodology remain explicit.
Bee-plant interaction records can benefit from geographic and taxonomic occurrence context, while occurrence records alone do not establish interaction relationships.
Interaction-network data and soil biodiversity observations can contribute to broader ecosystem context, but there is no direct organismal linkage asserted.
